Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: Limited US Reputation and Promotional Tour Challenges (1971)
facts.body: In 1971, David Bowie was only "big-ish" in Britain and had "absolutely no reputation whatsoever" in the United States. Due to immigration and work permit issues, he was unable to officially tour for *The Man Who Sold the World*, instead conducting private concerts for journalists from his hotel room bed. "Bowie was only big-ish in Britain and had absolutely no reputation whatsoever in the United States."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Dave Marsh Coins "Punk Rock" in Print (May 1971)
facts.body: Writer Dave Marsh is credited with the first printed use of the phrase "punk rock" in May 1971. He used it in an article about the reformation of the 60s garage band Question Mark in the Mysterians, describing their reunion as "a landmark explosion of punk rock," a crucial moment in the term's evolution. "And the guy who seems to have done it first in print anyway was a writer named Dave Marsh."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Early "Punk Rock" as an Aesthetic (1971)
facts.body: In 1971, "punk rock" was understood more as an aesthetic or attitude than a defined sound, primarily used by writers and critics rather than musicians themselves. Early artists like Alice Cooper and Kiss were even considered "punk rock" by some, indicating the term's initial broad and somewhat unfocused application. "In 1971 punk rock was more of a aesthetic than a sound. It was a phrase used by writers and critics not musicians."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: Punk Rock

facts.title: Tax Exile in France (1971)
facts.body: In 1971, The Rolling Stones were forced to move to France as "tax exiles" because the British government was taxing 93% of their earnings, leaving them with only 7%. This event inspired the title of their album "Exile on Main Street." "In 1971, the Rolling Stones were required to pay 93% of all their earnings in taxes. They got to keep 7% of what they earned, 93%. And that's why they moved to France as tax exiles, which is why the next album was called exile on Main Street."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer
facts.name: The Rolling Stones

"It was designed by John Pash, and he was paid a grand total of, wait for it, 50 pounds for it."

facts.body: In 1971, members Dennis Wilson and Carl Wilson recorded public service announcements to encourage young people to register and vote after the ratification of the 26th Amendment. One of the few ways it's possible to change things around in this world is through the vote."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Ann Arbor John Sinclair Freedom Rally (1971)
facts.body: On December 10th, 1971, John and Yoko performed at a concert in Ann Arbor, Michigan, to support musician and activist John Sinclair, who was sentenced to 9.5-10 years for selling marijuana to undercover officers. The event, which also featured Stevie Wonder, Bob Seger, Allen Ginsberg, Bobby Seale, and Jerry Rubin, cost $3 for admission and was broadcast on Michigan radio. An article in the *New York Daily News* highlighted the event's "immediate inescapable impact" regarding the "potential power of the new young voter," and remarkably, John Sinclair was set free the following Monday morning. "John and Yoko performed at a concert in Ann Arbor, Michigan that was on behalf of Johnson Claire, a local musician and a political activist who happened to make the very unfortunate decision to sell marijuana to two undercover police officers."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 21 - Rockin' the Vote - 70s Rock and Politics

facts.title: Glam Rock Catalyst (1971)
facts.body: In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on the hugely important British TV show "Top of the Pops." During this performance, Marc Bolan, the band's frontman, wore satin clothes and was covered with glitter dust, an event that David Bowie watched at home and found "brilliant," marking it as "the beginning of glam rock" and inspiring Bowie to pursue a similar direction. "In March 1971, T-Rex appeared on top of the pops, the hugely important British TV show."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Glam Rock Craze Initiation (1971)
facts.body: Mark Bolan, at 24 years old, initiated the glam rock craze when T. Rex appeared on Top of the Pops in 1971, showcasing glitter, satin pants, and a sexually heightened, androgynous look. This performance was watched by a nine-year-old David Evans (The Edge) in Dublin, who described Bolan as magical. "Mark Bowlin was magical but also sexually heightened and androgynous with this glitter and makeup."

facts.body: In the fall of 1971, Rick Nelson and his band performed at a nostalgic multi-act concert at New York's Madison Square Garden, sharing the bill with classic rock and rollers like Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley, and Bobby Rydell. facts.title: Untitled Fourth Album
facts.body: This album was notable for its almost complete lack of traditional liner notes, a deliberate choice to build mystery and myth around the band. The cover featured no title and the band's name was absent. The gatefold sleeve contained only a painting of "the Hermit" figure. Basic information and four unique "root symbols" representing each band member were found only on the inner paper sleeve, alongside minimal song lyrics. "Led Zeppelin's fourth album had almost zero in the way of liner notes."

facts.body: In the 1990s, a copy of Led Zeppelin's fourth album, which includes "Stairway to Heaven," was observed selling for $24.99 on CD. This price was equivalent to nearly $40 in contemporary money, significantly more expensive than the vinyl version which could be purchased for around $6.99 on sale, despite the album having already sold over 20 million copies and having long recouped its costs. "I recall being in a store in the 90s and seeing a copy of Led Zeppelin's fourth album, you know, in the one with the stairway to heaven on it. Selling for $24.99."

facts.body: Considered the band's second official album, named after a trip to Mallorca, this work allowed Can to pursue a more daring sonic path. Jaki Liebezeit's drums were in a "state of grace," acting as the sole anchor amidst a surrealist canvas of distortion, noise, electronic keyboards, and tape manipulation that created the band's signature musical landscape. This profoundly unusual double album showcased their unique compositional method, involving extensive improvisation sessions from which appealing segments were later cut and potentially enhanced with arrangements. The first vinyl focused on rhythm, concluding with the sublime 18-minute funk trance of "Halleluwah," which nearly anticipated drum and bass, while the second vinyl explored more abstract and cosmic themes with long tracks like "Aumgn" and "Peking O," revisiting the atonal spirit of Stockhausen. It is widely regarded as the band's most famous and acclaimed work, frequently appearing on lists of the greatest rock albums in history, offering a wilder, darker, and tenser form of psychedelia in contrast to Pink Floyd's meticulously constructed progressive approach, with its groovy rhythms and often dark sonic pollution serving as a clear reference for John Lydon's band PiL. facts.body: For years, Randy California of Spirit and later his estate claimed that Jimmy Page ripped off the guitar arpeggio from Spirit's instrumental "Taurus" for this song. facts.body: This song, recorded in the winter of 1971, moved Denver closer to country music, despite being a pop smash that reached number two on Billboard's Hot 100 in the summer of 1971. Its origin traces to December 1970 when Denver met Bill Danoff and Taffy Nivert (Fat City) in D.C., and the trio collaboratively wrote its bridge in an all-night session. They debuted it to a five-minute standing ovation at D.C.'s Cellar Door Club. Released as a single in the spring of 1971, it debuted at number 99 and took over four months to reach number two, prevented from reaching number one by the Bee Gees' "How Can You Mend a Broken Heart." This song established John Denver as a solo artist and defined his persona as earnest, folky, and homespun with a talent for melody. Surprisingly, it only reached number 50 on the Hot Country Singles chart, as the country audience was not initially very interested. "Take me home country roads turned out to be a pop smash eventually climbing to number two on billboards hot 100 in the summer of 71."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Invention of Mini Moog (1971)
facts.body: In 1971, Dr. Moog introduced the Mini Moog, an invention credited with making much of today's music possible. This synthesizer could perform almost everything its larger predecessors could, but was significantly smaller (a little bigger than a suitcase) and, crucially, much cheaper, making the technology accessible to a new generation of musicians, many of whom came of age during the punk era. "The big break came in 1971 when Dr. Mogue showed up again, this time with a new synthesizer design he called the Mini Mogue. This one invention made much of today's music possible."

facts.body: Originally released on the 1971 album 'Hunky Dory', "Changes" first climbed to number 66 in 1972. RCA reissued it in January 1975, promoting it as Bowie's ultimate statement of purpose, embodying his lyrical declaration of needing to be a "different man." However, this reissue stalled at number 41, just missing the American Top 40 again. "It was the second attempt to turn that classic song into a hit, originally released on Bowie's 1971 album, Hunky Dory, Changes had climbed as high as number 66, the first time in 1972."

facts.title: Founding and First Megastore (1971 - 1979)
facts.body: The first Virgin store was opened in January 1971 by Richard Branson, who would go on to found Virgin Records the following year. The company experienced rapid growth, leading to the opening of its first "Megastore" in 1979 on Oxford Street near Tottenham Court Road in London, situated just a few blocks from HMV's flagship store. "The first Virgin store opened in January 1971 by Richard Branson, who had later found Virgin Records a year later."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Virgin Megastores

facts.title: Madison Square Garden Concert Reception (1971)
facts.body: In the fall of 1971, Rick Nelson and his band performed at a nostalgic multi-act concert at New York's Madison Square Garden, sharing the bill with classic rock and rollers like Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley, and Bobby Rydell. Nelson and his band were poorly received by the "hippie crowd," who reportedly "sat on their hands" and even booed. This negative experience led Nelson to storm off stage and write his hit song "Garden Party." "But Rick Nelson and his band were not well received. The hippie crowd in attendance mostly sat on their hands, reportedly some even booed."

facts.body: Released on October 11th, 1971, this song became a single in the United States three months after the 26th Amendment was certified, reaching number three on the Billboard charts. It emerged as another global anthem for peace and was inspired by Yoko Ono's poetry from her 1964 book *Grapefruit*. While Lennon initially took sole songwriting credit, Yoko Ono finally received credit 48 years later in 2017. "In the middle of the night, imagine all the people living for today. Imagine there's no country, it isn't hard to do."

facts.body: George Harrison's song was involved in a long-running plagiarism case against The Chiffons' "He's So Fine" (1963). The judge ultimately ruled that Harrison was guilty of "subconscious plagiarism" or cryptomnesia, meaning he unconsciously replicated the melody, believing it to be an original composition, despite differences in key, arrangement, and instrumentation. The case, which started in 1971, was resolved in 1993, primarily over the ownership of the central melody and back royalties. "George Harrison got caught with this. Because it sounded way too much like this chiffon song from 1963."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
